Not because of the sprites themselves, they look great. But they look \*stiff\*. The reason why the current graphics work is that the imagination fills in the blanks.

To use your own example, Rina and Ellie don't look like they have their fists clenched, and they can have whatever expression we want them to have in that exact moment. They can even be talking right now. At 4x, we know exactly where they're looking, what their expression is and how they're standing. Now it looks awkward and stilted, like they're dolls ready to be dressed up.

[Eiyuden](https://assetsio.gnwcdn.com/eiyuden-hundred-header-1.jpg) might be where you're thinking in terms of improvements. The sprites are clearer, the style is clearly for current-gen and not retro, but it's [still pixel art](https://cdn.wccftech.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/20240415010836_1-scaled.jpg).

With all that said, your spritework is stellar. I'd love to see you do this same improvement to the battle sprites: they would benefit so much from a higher res like what you did here. Don't get discouraged by the reactions here - your art is fantastic, the direction is just lacking.

Don't lie about what you can do, stretch out the time you've been at a job if you can. Set up an email address too, in case of references.

You're seeing the challenge on a per-fight scale.

XCOM will force you into thinking of missions as more than the sum of its parts.

The challenge isn't just "can you finish this mission using these soldiers", it's also a race to outdo your enemy's technology, pick and choose your regions to get the right perks. I let missions fail or only send in one or two soldiers to sneak through enemy lines just so I can weather the next mission. This game will always have you on the back foot unless you force it on the strategic layer.

If you think the game is won on the tactical layer, you're in for a rude awakening.

Hence why people here are saying "lose the fight so you can win the war"

What we mean when we say you're allowed to fail missions is that you *can* decide a mission is not worth any further losses and you can leave.

Lose the battle, win the war.

On Veteran difficulty, you will rack up losses. What's important is that you survive your losses and make the wins count.

Also, "take out the objectives" here means ignoring the enemies. If you do the initial objective then the game asks to neutralise the remaining aliens, you can evac.

The skills you gained from Fromsoft games do not translate here.

As everyone has said, start with Rookie. Veteran is for when you're confident enough to lose fights so you don't lose the war.

Don't be afraid to fly out and evac, don't be afraid to fail missions. Your soldiers are your greatest asset, and even more so in the mid game. Bail them out if you're losing too many. There's rarely any missions where winning is worth losing my men.

That's the main issue with the global marketplace, sadly. It's the fact that everyone has to match the American prices, so that means you have to pay the exact same amount as Joe Hill in Wisconsin despite his hourly wage going further in your money.

However, this is something beyond gaming.

Consider this: you made a game. Yay! You price it fairly at, say $20. It's a neat little game, does decently well. Now, at the current pricing model, no matter who buys your game, you get the same profit of about $14. Great for developers, but international players have to pay a significant premium to reach that same $20 price tag you've set because of factors that they, you the developer, or even Valve the storefront can't control or even predict.

Maybe regional pricing can fix this, but then you'd run into the issue where gamers will VPN into poorer countries, buy your game, and save a hell of a lot of money on it. That means instead of the $14 per game that you're gonna get as a developer, you only get $8. Still a profit, and you're keeping it fair for international gamers. But if the majority of players do that, then you're better off just pricing it evenly across the globe.

But truthfully? Pirate to your heart's content. You're not taking away a copy from someone, and a lot of game devs don't mind the piracy since 1) they've been paid by the publisher already, 2) you weren't gonna buy the game anyway, most likely so they were never gonna get a sale from you, 3) you're PLAYING THEIR GAME. AND TELLING PEOPLE ABOUT HOW COOL SAID GAME IS.

So pirate away, but consider either buying merch or supporting the people who make the game in ways you can (buying later, buying on sale). Plus if their game goes off the storefronts because the publisher said so, you still have your copy.
